chapter.name: Linear Inequalities
chapter.blurb: This chapter introduces inequalities -- statements using <, >, <= or >= -- and classifies them as numerical or literal, strict or slack, and linear or not. It gives the two rules for solving a linear inequality in one variable, including reversing the sign on multiplying or dividing by a negative number, and solves such inequalities over the natural numbers, integers and reals with the solutions shown on a number line. It closes with double inequalities, systems of two inequalities in one variable, and word problems on marks, numbers, lengths, temperature and mixtures.

scope_in.item: Recognise an inequality and classify it as numerical, literal or double, and as strict (<, >) or slack (<=, >=)
Identify linear inequalities in one variable (ax + b < 0 etc., a not 0) and in two variables (ax + by < c etc., a and b not 0), and tell them apart from quadratic inequalities, which are not linear
Translate a statement ('less than', 'at most', 'up to', 'at least') into an inequality in one or two variables, without solving the two-variable case
State what a solution and the solution set of an inequality in one variable are, and find solutions by trial
Apply Rule 1 (add or subtract equal numbers) and Rule 2 (multiply or divide by a positive number; reverse the sign for a negative number) to an inequality
Solve a linear inequality in one variable when x is a natural number, an integer or a real number, and give the solution set in each case
Solve linear inequalities with brackets and fractions for real x and write the solution set in interval notation
Represent the solutions of a one-variable inequality on a number line: open circle for < or >, dark circle for <= or >=, line darkened to the left or right
Solve a double inequality such as -8 <= 5x - 3 < 7 by operating on all three parts, reversing the signs when dividing by a negative
Solve a system of two linear inequalities in one variable by taking the common values, and show the solution on a number line

Solve word problems that lead to linear inequalities in one variable: averages and marks, consecutive odd or even numbers, side lengths and cut lengths, temperature conversion, IQ and acid or boric-acid mixtures

concepts.name: Inequalities: meaning, types and formation
concepts.description: What an inequality is; numerical, literal and double inequalities; strict and slack inequalities; linear inequalities in one and in two variables versus quadratic ones; writing an inequality from a statement.
concepts.idea: Two real numbers or two algebraic expressions related by <, >, <= or >= form an inequality. Many statement problems ('at most', 'at least', 'less than') translate into inequalities rather than equations.
concepts.rule: < and > give strict inequalities; <= and >= give slack inequalities. ax + b < 0 (a not 0) is linear in one variable; ax + by < c (a, b not 0) is linear in two variables; ax^2 + bx + c > 0 is quadratic, not linear.
concepts.example: Registers at Rs 40 and pens at Rs 20 bought with Rs 120: 40x + 20y <= 120, a slack linear inequality in two variables.

concepts.name: Solutions, the two rules, and solving over natural numbers, integers and reals
concepts.description: Solution and solution set of an inequality in one variable; the addition rule and the multiplication rule with sign reversal for negatives; how the solution set changes with the set x is taken from.
concepts.idea: A solution is a value of the variable that makes the inequality true. The same inequality has different solution sets over the natural numbers, the integers and the real numbers.
concepts.rule: Rule 1: equal numbers may be added to or subtracted from both sides. Rule 2: both sides may be multiplied or divided by the same positive number; with a negative number the sign of inequality is reversed.
concepts.example: 30x < 200 gives x < 20/3: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} over natural numbers, {..., -1, 0, 1, ..., 6} over integers.

concepts.name: Solving linear inequalities for real x and showing solutions on a number line
concepts.description: Solving one-variable linear inequalities with brackets and fractions over the reals, writing the solution set as an interval, and representing it on a number line.
concepts.idea: Over the reals the solution set of a linear inequality is an interval running without end in one direction, shown on a number line by a circle at the end point and a darkened ray.
concepts.rule: Clear brackets and fractions (multiply every term), collect x, and reverse the sign when dividing by a negative. For x < a or x > a use an open circle at a; for x <= a or x >= a use a dark circle; darken left for less than, right for greater than.
concepts.example: (5 - 2x)/3 <= x/6 - 5 gives 10 - 4x <= x - 30, so -5x <= -40 and x >= 8: the interval [8, infinity).

concepts.name: Double inequalities and systems of two inequalities in one variable
concepts.description: Solving double inequalities such as -8 <= 5x - 3 < 7 and systems of two linear inequalities in one variable, and showing the common solutions on a number line.
concepts.idea: A double inequality is two inequalities that must hold together. A system is solved by solving each inequality and taking the values of x common to both.
concepts.rule: Apply the same operation to all three parts of a double inequality; dividing by a negative reverses both signs. For a system, the solution is the overlap of the two graphs on the number line.
concepts.example: 3x - 7 < 5 + x gives x < 6 and 11 - 5x <= 1 gives x >= 2, so the system has solution 2 <= x < 6.

concepts.name: Word problems leading to linear inequalities in one variable
concepts.description: Translating statement problems on averages and marks, consecutive odd or even numbers, lengths, temperature conversion, IQ and mixtures into inequalities in one variable and interpreting the solution.
concepts.idea: Phrases such as 'at least', 'at most', 'more than' and 'between' become inequality signs; the solution must then be read back in the context (whole numbers, odd numbers, lengths).
concepts.rule: Let x be the unknown, write each condition as an inequality, solve, and keep only the values that fit the context. 'At least' is >=, 'at most' is <=, 'more than' is >, 'less than' is <.
concepts.example: Marks 62 and 48, average at least 60: (62 + 48 + x)/3 >= 60 gives x >= 70, so the minimum is 70 marks.

Her numbers are right, but the end values are not allowed: at x = 900 the mixture is exactly 25% and at x = 562.5 exactly 30%, and both conditions are strict.
